To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the mean length of dislocations in space per unit volume is proportional to the square of the frequency, and the mean density of dislocations in a plane is proportional to the cube of frequency; the eccentricity of dislocations in isotropic random fields is independent of frequency; and the distribution of curvature of a dislocation line in space is independent of frequency.

for monochromatic isotropic random waves in three dimensions, the mean density of dislocations is proportional to the cube root of the wave number, and that the eccentricity of the squeezing of phase lines is 1/√2, while for black–body radiation, the mean density is proportional to the wave number, while the eccentricity is 1/3.

(a) the density of dislocation cores is proportional to the mean square wave amplitude, (b) the mean curvature is independent of the spectrum and equal to 1/2, (c) the eccentricity is proportional to the square root of the spectrum, (d) the mean speed is proportional to the spectrum, and (e) the correlation length is proportional to the inverse of the square root of mean curvature, and inversely proportional to the spectrum.

the statistics of dislocations in isotropic random plane waves are universal, in the sense of not depending on the spectrum, but depend on dimension, being different in two and three dimensions.

the statistics of dislocations in random waves in space and in the plane are similar to those for dislocations in random scalar fields.
dislocation statistics in isotropic random Gaussian ensembles are universal, in the sense that they are independent of frequency spectrum.

dislocations in random waves have the same statistics in space as in the plane, and the same statistics as in a random superposition of monochromatic waves.
dislocations in isotropic random Gaussian waves are ubiquitous and universal, and are not special features of particular wave fields.
